title: The week the agents moved in
summary: A burglar with an army of AI agents, a lab that measured its own office, and a shopper with no body. Three stories from one week, and the one question underneath them.
music: Warm late-night jazz podcast theme: brushed drums, upright bass walk, muted trumpet hook, confident and calm, no vocals.
lines: This is After the Headline, from AI Broadsheet. I'm Jack.
And I'm Nora. We're both synthetic voices, by the way, reading a script our newsroom wrote and checked. Every number you'll hear is in the sources, linked in the show notes.
This week, three stories landed within about forty-eight hours of each other. A hacker, a hiring report, and a payments company. And they're really one story.
The week the agents moved in. Let's start with the burglar.

Reuters, October nineteenth. A security researcher named Snorre Fagerland, at a firm called NorForge, was scanning the internet for exposed copies of an open-source AI platform called Cairn. He found about two dozen being used for malicious work.
And one of them belonged to a single hacker who, according to Reuters, broke into the websites of more than a hundred companies. John Deere. SharkNinja.
Here's the detail that stopped me. The instructions were short. Fewer than a hundred Chinese characters. Then the agents did the rest.

More than twelve hundred sites tried, starting September twenty-fifth. A typical successful break-in took about twenty-three hours of automated probing. And Fagerland's estimate for the whole campaign was about five thousand dollars in AI tokens. Roughly fifty dollars a break-in.
And it apparently ran on DeepSeek and Anthropic's Claude Code, according to the researcher. I'll note that our newsroom uses AI tools too, including Claude.
Good. What did the companies say?
Deere said it took remediation actions and had no indication sensitive information was accessed. SharkNinja said the site held only product support information and the threat was contained.

So the lesson isn't that AI hacks better than people. The researcher said it's not script kiddie stuff, sure. The lesson is the price. Patience used to be expensive. Twenty-three hours of trying doors used to cost a person twenty-three hours.
Now it costs fifty dollars. Which means every forgotten server, every old control panel nobody patched, is suddenly worth trying.
Story two is quieter, and I think it's bigger. Anthropic published a report about its own workforce.
A lab measuring what its own machine did to its own office.

In its technical teams, juniors were twenty-seven percent of new hires in early twenty twenty-five. Now, nine percent. Since March, its AI agents have logged more hours than its people. By August, six agent hours for every human hour.

And the humans are in more meetings. Up twenty percent per employee, from calendar data. In an internal survey, one in five said their job had shifted from doing the work to managing Claudes. Their word.
To be fair to the report, it calls Anthropic a special case. A company that has molded its whole workflow around AI. And it says more code does not necessarily mean better code.

Which is honest. But here's what I keep thinking about. Every senior engineer was once a junior engineer. The junior years are where judgment gets built. If the first rung goes, who checks the machine in ten years?
That's the real question. Not whether the agent can do the work. Whether anybody will still learn how to tell when it's wrong.
Stripe says purchases made by AI agents through Link, its payment service, grew thirty-eight times in September. Payment volume, twenty times.
And the total? Stripe won't say. The growth started from a small base, which means big multipliers can hide small numbers.

About seventy agents were using it when Stripe looked. Around two hundred now, according to Stripe executive Dan Hill. Most purchases are about a hundred dollars. Retail is the biggest category, then travel.
And the safety catch is actually good design. The agent never gets your real card number. Link issues a separate sixteen-digit number, and you can set a spending limit.
So, three stories. An agent that breaks in. Agents that do the junior work. Agents that spend the money. What's the thread?
Delegation. For two years we talked about AI that answers. This week was about AI that acts. And when something acts for you, the question changes from is it smart to who's accountable.
For a website owner, it's the forgotten server. For a company, it's the junior you didn't hire. For you, it's the purchase you didn't read.
Set the limit. Read the receipt. Keep the final yes.

That's After the Headline. The full stories, the sources, and our noir video series, The Sir Jack Files, are at AI Broadsheet dot com. And if you want this every morning, the newsletter sign-up is right there.
